extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, scientific method, and anyone learning critical reasoning/observation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying and avoiding errors in the observation stage of proof (non-observation and mal-observation), including what kinds of instances and circumstances are commonly overlooked, how inferences are mistaken for perceptions, and how these mistakes mislead induction and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-observation (overlooking facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-observation is when all the error consists in overlooking, or neglecting, facts or particulars which ought to have been observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-observation may be of instances or of circumstances; it produces an insufficiency of evidence which vitiates otherwise just conclusions. Examples: accepting a fortune-teller because one ignores falsified predictions; failing to notice collusion that explains fulfilled predictions. The error is negative (something unseen) rather than a positive mis-estimate of observed evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-observation — overlooking instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-observation of instances occurs when relevant cases that would alter a generalization are not noticed or remembered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This leads to unjustified induction from insufficient evidence. Example: belief in a prophet kept alive because people remember the hits but not the misses. Remedies: seek out contrary instances; avoid generalizing from only remembered/striking examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-observation — overlooking circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-observation of circumstances happens when particular cases are observed but important concomitant conditions are ignored, producing false singular propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: phlogiston theory ignored gaseous combustion products; cures credited to a mysterious powder when healing depended on keeping wounds undisturbed; mercury seemingly effective because the disease's rapid fatal cases occur before treatment. Guidance: examine and record all relevant circumstances and possible confounders in each instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preconceived opinion bias
rubrics_metrics.description: A preconceived opinion is the greatest cause of non-observation: when people start with a theory they commonly fail to notice facts that contradict it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations include resistance to Copernican evidence and travellers who see only what accords with prior beliefs. To avoid: deliberately seek observations that could refute your hypothesis; design tests rather than rely on casual observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective memory / affirmative-instance bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind is more moved by and remembers affirmative instances than negative ones, leading to accumulation of confirming anecdotes while neglecting disconfirming events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains the persistence of superstitions and the fame of occasional successful predictions. Countermeasure: place more weight on negative instances when forming axioms; actively collect negative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of chance (need for adequate instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent coincidences can mislead unless enough instances are collected to eliminate chance as an explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A certain number of casual coincidences will occur between unconnected events; credible induction requires sampling sufficient to rule out chance. Plan observations to test for and eliminate random coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mal-observation (mistaking inference for perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mal-observation occurs when something seen is seen wrong — typically by mistaking inference for direct perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perceptions are infallible as perceived; error arises when inference is presented as perception. Example: people 'saw' the sun rise and set and took that appearance as perceptual proof for geocentrism. Remedy: clearly distinguish and label what is directly perceived versus what is inferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to separate perception and inference in testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrators and witnesses often confound their inferences with what they actually perceived, producing unreliable descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced cross-examiners know witnesses mix hypothesis with observation; less educated observers tend to embed more conjecture in their accounts. When evaluating testimony, ask what part rests on consciousness (perception) and what part on inference; treat the latter as questionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden or unobserved causal factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Important causal factors may be unobserved or hidden, leading to wrong causal attributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: phlogiston overlooked gaseous residues; apparent cures due to rest/regimen rather than the promoted remedy; sympathetic powder 'cures' due to wound dressings. Guidance: look for unseen processes or concurrent treatments that could explain observed effects; attempt to isolate variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on immediate visible effects over diffuse/indirect effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers tend to notice immediate, concentrated, obvious effects and overlook widely diffused or deeper effects that may oppose them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic example: lavish spending visibly benefits tradespeople (apparent employment) while savings (less visible) can produce equal or greater employment via investment. Evaluate both short-term visible impacts and longer-term, indirect consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer competence and habit (discipline of observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deficiencies in an observer's training, attention, or habits of analysis make certain sorts of facts especially likely to be missed or misreported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text distinguishes errors from mere casual inattention: logic concerns what kinds of instances observers generally miss. Training (e.g., in analytic description, careful sensory reporting) reduces the tendency to pass over sensations and substitute inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of negative instances in establishing axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: In forming and testing axioms, negative instances have greater force than affirmative ones: the establishment of a true axiom often depends on noticing negatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'in omni Axiomate vero constituendo, major vis est instantiæ negativæ.' When constructing general laws, actively search for disconfirming cases rather than only accumulating supporting anecdotes.
